No new matter is added by way of these amendments, entry of which is earnestly

solicited. Further, these amendments require no additional search on the part of the Office, do not raise any new issues, and place the claims in condition for allowance. The M.P.E.P. provides that "any amendment," including an after-final amendment, "that will place the application either in condition for allowance or in better form for appeal may be entered." See M.P.E.P. § 714.12.
Applicant also respectfully notes that a request for AFCP 2.0 is being filed concurrently herewith. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests entry of the claim amendments.
Upon entry of these amendments, claims 17, 18, and 21-39 are pending with claims 28- 39 being withdrawn.
Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of the Office Action mailed August 20, 2024, in view of the foregoing amendments and the remarks provided below
I. Claim Interpretation - 35 USC §112

Applicant notes that the Examiner has interpreted various features of the claims under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f). Applicant does not concede that 35 U.S.C. §112(f) applies to the features of the claims as filed. Nevertheless, Applicant amends various claims such that 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) does not apply.
II. Claim Rejections - 35 USC §103

Claims 17, 18, and 23-27 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 for being unpatentable over U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2009/0171234 to Gurewitsch (hereinafter "Gurewitsch") in view of U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2014/0114193 to Anthony (hereinafter "Anthony") in view of U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2007/0167819 to Osborn (hereinafter "Osborn) in view of U.S. Patent No. 6,045,517 to Williams (hereinafter "Williams"), in view of US Patent Application Publication No. 2003/0164708 Park (hereinafter "Park"), in view of International Application Publication WO 00/17863 to Beane (hereinafter "Beane"), and in view of U.S. Patent No. 6,258,024 to Van Der Weegan (hereinafter "Van Der Weegan").

Claim 20 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 for being unpatentable over Gurewitsch, Anthony, Osborn, Williams, Park, Beane, Van Der Weegan, in view of US Patent Application Publication No. 2012/0187000 Kahn (hereinafter "Kahn"). In the herewith amended claims, the limitations of claim 20 have been included into claim 17 and discussion of the rejections pertaining to claim 20 will be considered in the arguments for claim 17.
Claims 21 and 22 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 for being unpatentable over
Gurewitsch, Anthony, Osborn, Williams, Van Der Weegan, in view of U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2013/0217979 to Blackadar (hereinafter "Blackadar").

Applicant respectfully disagrees. All of the presently pending claim recite an elongate probe that is an electrical impedance spectroscopy probe suitable for investigation the electrical conductivity of cervical tissue. None of the presently cited references, alone or in combination, teach or suggest the combination of elements and the resulting structure of the present claims.

The probe of claim 17 is used to measure cervical bioimpedance. To measure cervical bioimpedance, the probe must reach the cervix via a patient's vagina. Each patient's anatomy is different. The patient's anatomy and their orientation during exam effect on the gravitational force on the tip of the probe.

There are historical challenges to such measurement of bioimpedance because the values of the readings are so small. Accurate force measurement, which is affected by the actual gravitational forces of the probe tip, makes the measurement of cervical bioimpedance possible. None of the cited references singly or in combination account for or compensate for gravitational force on the probe tip. The ability to compensate for the gravitational forces allows for the measurement of force at much smaller levels previously not seen in the art. There is no available device that can be used for the purpose that the claimed device can be used for because such available devices cannot measure at the small dimensions that the claimed device can. This device thus has satisfied a long felt need in the field, which is an indication of patentability.
In view of the above and further discussion below, Applicant submits that claims 17, 18 and 21-27 are allowable over the cited reference.

Claim 17 recites a tip with an EEPROM that has the tip mass stored thereon. As such, the device does not require calibration to compensate for gravity acting on the probe tip, apart from the calibration of the load cell at device manufacture because, as the mass of the probe is determined beforehand using a balance and the numeric mass value. Thus, with live gravity and load cell measurements and known mass of the probe tip it is possible to generate fully compensated tip force measurements without further calibration.
The Office Action cites Gurewitsch as teaching a device for measuring bioimpedance of cervical tissue and acquiesces that Gurewitsch does not appear to explicitly teach the apparatus

capable of determining a force Ftip. The Office Action alleges that it would have been obvious to replace the spring arrangement of Gurewitsch (as shown in Fig. 12 and described in 0102) with the force sensor and associated components of Anthony (e.g. accelerometer, etc.), for the purpose of obtaining quantitative data about the conditions under which the device was used (Anthony: 005), including data on the degree of axial loading on the probe tip, to thereby account for the conditions based on quantitative analysis and processing (Anthony: 0084), instead of relying on maintaining a "general" continuity of contact using the spring of Gurewitsch ( 0102).

The Applicant respectfully contends that the probe tip of Anthony is not described as replaceable or interchangeable. Thus, it would not have been obvious to store the mass of a specific probe tip on the tip, to enable mass-compensated measurement with different tips, in combination with all other features of the claims.
Moreover, the Office Action alleges that Kahn as teaching an EEPROM to store probe calibration parameters. However, Applicant does not believe Kahn is analogous to the present claims.
Kahn relates to a sensor for detecting concentration of an analyte in a sample. This is

cherry picking of features from a field of art that would not be consulted by one of ordinary skill in the art, nor does Kahn solve a problem with which the present invention is concerned. That is, Kahn would only be considered using hindsight given the present application. Accordingly, Applicant submits that claim 17 is not rendered obvious by the teaching of Kahn in combination with Gurewitsch-Anthony-Osborn-Park-Beane-Van Der Weegen and respectfully request the rejection be withdrawn.

Regarding Claims 18 and 21-27, while Applicant does not agree with or concede to this rejection, Applicant notes that it is axiomatic that dependent claims are non-obvious under Section 103 if the independent claims from which they depend are non-obvious. See In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071, 1076 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Thus, because independent claim 17 is novel and non- obvious, at least for the reasons argued above, it follows that all dependent claims are non- obvious and in condition for allowance as well.
III. Double Patenting

The claims have been provisionally rejected on the grounds of nonstatutory double patenting as being unpatentable over claims 1-9 of U.S. Patent No. 11,660,046 Anumba (hereinafter "Anumba") in view of Gurewitsch, Anthony, Osborn, Williams, Van Der Weegan, Park, Kahn, Blackadar as outlined previously. The applicant respectfully requests the grounds of rejection be deferred until all other matters of substance have been resolved.

Applicant asks that all claims be examined in view of the amendments to the claims. The absence of additional comments regarding the Office Action does not signify agreement with or concession of any characterization or requirement. In addition, because the arguments and comments herein may not be exhaustive, there may be additional arguments and comments that have not been expressed.
